newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -Squeezing year-end gains from Europe.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -Squeezing year-end gains from Europe.

text.p: By Jacqueline Thorpe,
Investors looking to pack last minute gains into their bond portfolios before year-end should cut duration in high yielding European markets, analysts said on Tuesday.
The long end of the British gilt market also offers potential for a year-end boost, analysts said.

"Probably the best risk-adjusted returns come from short-dated paper in some of the European markets," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London, citing Italy, Spain and Sweden for the best potential returns.
"Although the Bundesbank is most unlikely to cut interest rates again, there is still scope for rate cuts in a number of countries of Europe," Edmonds said.
Gordon Ross, head of global institutional fixed income for Chase Asset Management (London) Ltd, agreed.

The long end of high yielding markets have rallied all summer, pushing their yields closer to core German Bunds, amid enthusiasm over the process of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), Ross said.
That area of the curve would now be subject to increasing volatility while the short-end offered a safer haven, he said.
"You're going to get the benefits of reduced short-term rates and the continued convergence play without the volatility at the very long end," he said.
Italy has the most scope for spread narrowing at the short end, Edmonds said, even after the Bank of Italy cut its discount rate by 0.75 percentage to 7.50 percent last week.
He expected the gap between two-year Italian and German paper to slim around 50 basis points by year-end from around 370 now.
"I think the Bank of Italy will want to cut interest rates once the budget is passed and once the lira is ensconced in the ERM (Exchange Rate Mechanism)," he said.

The rate outlook for Spain is similar, according to Ross. He expects interest rates to fall before the end of the year, despite the discovery this summer of a 721 billion peseta gap in Spain's 1995 accounts.
"That weakens the case somewhat but they still require some form of impetus," he said.
Adrian Owens, European economist at Julius Baer Investments in London, said Sweden could also trim rates further, despite a major rate-cutting offensive already this year.
But Owens said gilts too held potential at the long end after lagging the high yielding market this year amid uncertainty about Britain's EMU aspirations.

He forecast the 10-year yield spread to narrow to 150 over the next few months from 169 currently as the rising British currency cooled inflation prospects and limited the need for higher interest rates. Sterling has gained more than six percent on the mark since early August.
"That has in many ways improved the outlook for gilts and as yet the gilt market hasn't really reacted," he said.

Ross at Chase Asset Management preferred three-to-five-year Irish government bonds over gilts for a short-term fillip. Gilts would be prone to political shenanigans ahead of a general election due by the end of May 1997.

"If anyone is going to meet the (EMU) criteria they (the Irish) are, and you have had added liquidity there over the course of this year as they've allowed more of the global securities houses to be involved with auctions and making markets," he said.
